A=[13−3−1],Σ=[4002] Consider the matrices A and Σ shown above. Given that A=UΣVT is a singular value decomposition of A, which of the following could be the matrices U and V?

a
U=[313213−213313] and V=[213313−313213]
b
U=[1212−1212] and V=[12−121212]
c
U=[1525−2515] and V=[25−151525]
d
U=[1525−2515] and V=[2515−1525]
e
U=[121212−12] and V=[12−121212]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's find the singular value decomposition of A using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute ATA: ATA=[13−3−1]T[13−3−1]=[1−33−1][13−3−1]=[106610]

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=4 and σ2=2.

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of A (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ATA):

    • For λ1=σ12=16, we have ATA−16I=[106610]−16[1001]=[−666−6]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (ATA−16I)v=0 gives a unit eigenvector
      v1=[1212].

    • For λ2=σ22=4, we have ATA−4I=[106610]−4[1001]=[6666]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (ATA−4I)v=0 gives a unit eigenvector
      v2=[−1212].

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of A: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of U as follows:

    • First, we compute u1: u1=1σ1Av1=14[13−3−1][1212]=14[22−22]=[12−12]

    • Then, we compute u2: u2=1σ2Av2=12[13−3−1][−1212]=12[22]=[1212]

Finally, we construct the matrices U and V:

U=[1212−1212],V=[12−121212]

content.knowledge_point: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
content.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=4$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=2.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=16,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-16I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]-16[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 6 \\ 6 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-16I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-4I & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 6 & 10\end{aligned}]-4[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}6 & 6 \\ 6 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-4I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2} \\ -2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}\sqrt{2} \\ \sqrt{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

decision.explanation: Option b has orthogonal U=V. Their columns (1,1)ᵀ/√2 and (−1,1)ᵀ/√2 are eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues 5 and 3, respectively. Thus AV=UΣ and A=UΣVᵀ.

after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
after.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

a
U=[213−313313213] and V=[313−213213313]
b
U=[12−121212] and V=[12−121212]
c
U=[310−110110310] and V=[110−310310110]
d
U=[−12−12−1212] and V=[12−121212]
e
U=[110−310310110] and V=[310−110110310]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's find the singular value decomposition of A using the usual algorithm.

  • Step 1. Compute ATA: ATA=[4114]T[4114]=[4114][4114]=[178817]

  • Step 2. Find the singular values: From the matrix Σ, we deduce that σ1=5 and σ2=3.

  • Step 3. Find the right singular vectors of A (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ATA):

    • For λ1=σ12=25, we have ATA−25I=[178817]−25[1001]=[−888−8]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (ATA−25I)v=0 gives a unit eigenvector
      v1=[1212].

    • For λ2=σ22=9, we have ATA−9I=[178817]−9[1001]=[8888]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (ATA−9I)v=0 gives a unit eigenvector
      v2=[−1212].

  • Step 4. Find the left singular vectors of A: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of U as follows:

    • First, we compute u1: u1=1σ1Av1=15[4114][1212]=15[5252]=[1212]

    • Then, we compute u2: u2=1σ2Av2=13[4114][−1212]=13[−3232]=[−1212]

Finally, we construct the matrices U and V:

U=[12−121212],V=[12−121212]

content.knowledge_point: The Singular Value Decomposition of a 2x2 Matrix
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $Σ$ shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ which of the following could be the matrices $U$ and $V?$
content.worked_solution:
Let's find the singular value decomposition of $A$ using the usual algorithm.

- **Step 1.** Compute ${A}^{T}\,A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}]}^{T}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 2.** Find the singular values: From the matrix $Σ,$ we deduce that ${\sigma }_{1}=5$ and ${\sigma }_{2}=3.$

- **Step 3.** Find the right singular vectors of $A$ (i.e., the unit eigenvectors of ${A}^{T}\,A$):

- For ${\lambda }_{1}={\sigma }_{1}^{2}=25,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-25I & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{aligned}]-25[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-8 & 8 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-25I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}={\sigma }_{2}^{2}=9,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A-9I & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 8 \\ 8 & 17\end{aligned}]-9[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $({A}^{T}\,A-9I)v=0$ gives a unit eigenvector

$$
{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

- **Step 4.** Find the left singular vectors of $A$: Since we know the singular values and right singular vectors, we can compute the columns of $U$ as follows:

- First, we compute ${u}_{1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{1}}A{v}_{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Then, we compute ${u}_{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{2} & =\frac{1}{{\sigma }_{2}}A{v}_{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we construct the matrices $U$ and $V:$

$$
U=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$
